author: Britt Bowman
text:
Welcome back to #MythsAndMigrations: The Stories Behind the Myths!

In the spring, I wrote about Jason: the collector of wins, who never built a kingdom, killed by a beam falling from the very ship that was meant to be his legacy. I referenced POCitis then. Proof after proof, pilot after pilot, and never once the operating system underneath any of it.

Maybe I told the wrong part of the myth.

There's an earlier scene that's rarely quoted. Partway through the voyage, the Argo lands on Mysia for fresh water and supplies. Hylas, barely more than a boy, wanders off to fill his jug at a spring and never comes back. The water nymphs pull him under, or he simply vanishes.

Heracles goes looking for him and doesn't return either, but the wind turns favorable, the crew grows restless with the wait, and someone gives the order to raise the sail.

They leave. Not out of cruelty. Out of momentum. The voyage has somewhere else to be, and waiting on two men who might never resurface costs more than the mission can spare. Nobody on that ship set out to abandon anyone. They just had a destination, and a schedule, and a story about the Golden Fleece that required forward motion more than it required loyalty to whoever happened to be standing on the shore when the tide turned.

I told myself I was done talking about being laid off, but the irony was just too significant to leave untouched as I revisit this myth.

In June, ServiceNow told me, and everyone watching, that the layoffs were part of restructuring for an AI-native future. I wasn't in the room where that decision was made, and I know layoffs are rarely driven by a single, clean reason or a single label. But I also know what I wrote about POCitis, I know I was let go a few weeks later, and I can't unsee how precisely one predicts the other.

I wasn't replaced by a pilot. Nobody built a demo that did my job better. I was left standing on the beach while the ship kept moving toward its next proof point, because stopping to account for the people already on board cost more than the story about AI required them to spend.

So, I went looking for what happened after the Argo disappeared over the horizon. Heracles didn't end on that beach. Depending on the telling, he eventually returned to Argos or continued toward Colchis on foot. Either way, the ship leaving without him wasn't the end of his story. It was only the end of his role in Jason's.

And we know how the rest of that comparison turns out: Jason gets the Golden Fleece. Heracles becomes Heracles.

Being necessary to one voyage and being valuable aren't the same. Organizations make decisions about who they need for where they're going next, and from inside that decision, it's easy to experience it as a verdict on everything you built, knew, and were capable of doing. It isn't.

The wind turns. The sail goes up. The ship leaves without you.

And sometimes that's how you find out you were never supposed to spend the rest of your story on that ship.

author: Britt Bowman
text:
You make a couple of elaborate cakes, and everyone wants one. I'm now on the hook for a cake a month through the end of the year.

I'd never in 100 years hand someone a grocery store cake. So when we headed to Colorado in August, close to my BIL's birthday, I knew what I had to do.

Ridiculously, I pre-made white chocolate bark and toasted pistachio crunch at home and packed them in plastic takeaway containers with rubber bands wrapped around the lids, because that seemed sturdy enough.

It wasn't.

It opened a bit mid-flight in the checked luggage, and my kids' clothing was covered in pistachios. We had plenty left for the cake. What? I made a lot, and we smelled delicious.

We were on our way to Crestone. Population 141. One tiny grocery store and one health food market; neither was fully stocked with what I needed.

My MIL's kitchen has not a single cake pan, so I baked all four layers one at a time in a springform pan at over 8,000 feet. Obviously, I'd researched exactly what elevation does to a cake before I ever cracked an egg: bump the temperature up a little, cut back the baking powder, add a bit more liquid, and don't trust the sugar amount a normal recipe gives you. I adjusted everything, and it came out exactly the way I wanted.

I made an impossibly large amount of Swiss meringue buttercream that came out silky and glossy, but getting it there meant running a blow dryer around the outside of the bowl while I mixed, warming it just enough to melt out the last bit of graininess without turning it into soup. I packed a blow dryer in my suitcase specifically for this. Pro move.

I live for this part: baking like this is hypertechnical and hypertactical. My brain loves it. There's a right ratio, a right temperature, a right amount of time to let something rest, and getting all of it to line up feels like solving a puzzle with a delicious answer.

The lemon curd I made for this cake was the best I've ever made. The blackberry gin-and-tonic syrup was life-changing, and the blackberry filling was divine.

I had so much of both lemon curd and blackberry filling left over that, a couple of days later, I turned them into lemon-and-cream-cheese crepes with a blackberry topping and watched everyone at that table go silent as they savored those beautifully married flavors. (Pictures sadly not taken of my crepes!)

I love the technical part, but that's not why I keep doing this. I love watching someone realize a cake took this much time, effort, and thought just for them. I love that people love it. There's something about putting this much effort into a single dessert for one person that says something words don't, and I think that's the actual thing I'm addicted to, not the baking itself.

So yes, I've apparently signed myself up for a cake a month through the end of the year. Grandparents Day is coming! I don't think there's a version of this where I stop, and I'm not sure I want one.

author: Britt Bowman
text:
Okay, this is ridiculous. My face was on a billboard in Times Square last week, and because it’s 2026 and I post about AI constantly, I feel obligated to clarify that this is an actual photograph. Nobody prompted this into existence.

LeanData put me up there because I’m speaking at #OpsStars 2026 in San Francisco, October 5–6, alongside a pretty incredible group of #RevOps and #GTM leaders.

I knew the Times Square billboard was happening, but I assumed it'd be like a giant event ad with a carousel of featured speakers, or a blink-and-you'll-miss-it shot. It would have still been cool!

Then these pictures showed up, and I realized that was my face, my name, and the Britt Bowman LLC logo taking up the whole thing long enough for them to send me FIVE shots from different angles. Girl, what?!

My session's called “Why GTM Transformations Fail Once the Technology is Live,” which will surprise absolutely no one who has been following me for more than five minutes.

I’m talking about the part of transformation that starts after the implementation team says everything works. The AI's live, the workflows technically exist, everyone's been trained, and somehow the business still isn’t operating differently. That’s where I’ve spent a huge portion of my career, and I’m excited to get into what actually has to happen between “we deployed it” and “this changed the business.”

author: Britt Bowman
text:
Next week, I'm being flown to LA for my new client's customer event.

Imagine that. Less than 3 months ago, I was laid off from ServiceNow after 12 years. Now I'm being treated like an honored guest.

They're bringing me in to help drive their FY2027 GTM planning, so I'm not going out there to pitch anything.

I have no deck, no proposal, and no pre-built plan.

I'm going to sit with their customers and their execs and listen to how the business works before I say a single word about what should come next.

I'm excited for a few reasons:

> Being laid off to a full client book in under 3 months is nuts

> Being flown to their biggest event of the year speaks to how they feel about me

> Getting to know their customers, products, and executives before jumping in and helping them drive the rigor that's required to move upmarket is legitimately energizing

I don't know exactly what I'll find in LA yet, and I'm not going to pretend I do.

But I know I'll come back with a much clearer sense of what this company actually needs, and that's the whole point of going out there in person instead of just working off a call.

author: Britt Bowman
text:
I helped significantly increase conversion at a client without generating a single new lead.

We fixed what “qualified” meant.

The company had plenty of demand. It also had sophisticated GTM infrastructure. But there was a problem hiding beneath it all.

Sales used “qualified” to mean the moment a lead hit a certain score. Marketing used the same word to mean something closer to intent. And a separate reporting layer had been built around a third definition nobody remembered agreeing to.

So when a lead became “qualified,” what was supposed to happen next depended on which version of qualified you were using.

That’s a conversion problem often misread as just an operational or data quality issue.

You can generate all the demand in the world, but if the teams responsible for moving it toward revenue don't share the same definitions, they can't consistently make the same decisions or take the same actions.

We didn't start by changing the tech.

We agreed on what “qualified” actually meant. What evidence had to be present. Who owned the definition. When a lead crossed that threshold. What happened next.

Then we rebuilt the data and reporting around that shared definition.

The data error rate improved by 98%. The personal spreadsheets disappeared. But more importantly, conversion increased significantly because the GTM system could finally respond consistently to the demand already inside it.

Same teams. Same technology. Same leads.

A shared definition changed what happened to them.

This is why I get twitchy when the answer to a conversion problem is “we need more leads.”

Maybe.

But first, ask Sales, Marketing, and Ops to independently define “qualified.”

If you get three different answers, I'd fix that before spending another dollar generating demand.

author: Britt Bowman
text:
I helped a GTM organization improve their conversion from 2.5% to over 10% in the first quarter after launch by rebuilding operations from single leads to buying groups.

Before that, pipeline looked healthy on paper. Leads flowed in, opportunities got created, reps worked them.

But deals kept stalling in the same invisible place: somewhere between marketing handing off a “qualified” lead and sales actually engaging the real buying committee behind it.

Nobody could point to the exact stage killing revenue.

The instinct was to generate more leads and hire more reps to push volume through a gap nobody had actually located.

The real problem wasn't lead volume.

A single-threaded lead model doesn't match how B2B buying actually works: multiple people, multiple roles, one deal.

So we rebuilt the model around buying groups instead of individual contacts.

Marketing, sales, and customer success each got a defined role tied to a specific stage of that buying group's journey, not a vague handoff.

I've watched this same failure at 30,000-person scale and at 150-person scale.

The size changes.

The missing structure around the handoff doesn't.

If your team can tell you how many leads came in but not which stage is actually costing you revenue, more volume isn't the fix.

A real buying-groups model is.

author: Britt Bowman
text:
You know the best career advice I ever ignored? "Stay in your lane."

My career would suck if I'd listened.

Marketing stays in Marketing, Operations owns process, IT owns technology, Data owns... well, data, and AI belongs to whoever got "AI" added to their title.

Except every meaningful problem I've solved lived between those lanes.

A 30% data-error rate wasn't really a data problem.

I had to get into definitions, ownership, process, and human behavior before it moved.

Slow time-to-market wasn't just a Marketing problem.

I had to understand the whole system connecting people, process, data, and decisions.

$240MM in stalled pipeline didn't get solved by saying "that's Sales' lane."

I followed where revenue stopped moving instead.

Early in my career, I thought the professional thing to do was bring in the right stakeholder, hand the issue to whoever technically owned it, and respect the org chart. Just solve my piece and pass it along.

Unsurprisingly, I was terrible at that.

Because if the data problem is actually a definitions problem, you follow it.

If the marketing problem is actually a workflow problem, you follow it.

If revenue disappears between two functions, the space between them is the work.

I don't stay in my lane. I'm all over the road.

I stay with the problem until I understand the system producing it.

Where we're going, we don't need lanes.

author: Britt Bowman
text:
For more than a decade, I've been trying to get people to see the same thing: We have a people problem, not an AI problem.

Companies keep treating AI like a technology rollout. Buy the platform, run the pilot, and wait for results.

But AI is operational work, y'all.

It runs on definitions, ownership, decision rights, workflows, and feedback loops that already exist in your business, whether they're good or bad.

I was solving this problem in enterprise transformation long before anyone called it 'AI readiness' because GenAI didn't create the issue; it just made the consequences impossible to ignore.

Here's the pattern I keep watching play out: a company has messy data, unclear ownership, and process handoffs nobody actually agreed to, but instead of fixing that, they add AI on top of it. Huge surprise to everyone... the AI doesn't fix the mess.

It makes decisions faster on top of the mess, which means bad decisions now happen at scale instead of one at a time.

But I've also seen the fix work. Not from new tools, but from rebuilding the operating model underneath everything: who owns what, what words actually mean, how work really moves versus how the org chart says it moves.

There's no AI platform, new pilot, better prompt, extra dashboard, or additional agent that can replace shared definitions, explicit ownership, clear decision rules, and someone who actually understands how the business runs, but budgets keep chasing the next use case, the next automation, and the next proof of concept.

The unsexy stuff, the definitions and handoffs nobody wants to own, is the actual foundation everything else sits on.

We're deploying AI faster than we're building the organizational infrastructure it needs to make good decisions. We're automating ambiguity instead of eliminating it.

Fix the operating model.

Fix the ownership gaps.

Fix the handoffs.

Then hand the business to a machine, not before.

author: Britt Bowman
text:
Want to get your business up and running (and profitable!) in record time like I did? These are the 7 small habits that changed how I work forever:

1. I put everything where Future Me will trip over it. If I need to remember it, remembering cannot be the system.
2. I ask "what actually broke?" before trying to fix anything. The presenting problem and the real problem are rarely twins.
3. I define the words before I debate the strategy. Half of organizational dysfunction is people agreeing in different languages.
4. I intentionally build for the day I won't feel like doing it. Shoes out. Weights ready. File open. Friction removed in advance.
5. I don't wait to be nominated. If I can see the system that needs to exist, I start building it.
6. I make the invisible visible. Map the handoffs. Write down the assumptions. Find the place where ownership disappears or gets murky.
7. I keep asking what I can subtract. A surprising amount of progress comes from removing something that never needed to exist.

None of these are particularly impressive, but that's probably why they work.

I've spent most of my career solving enormous, complicated problems.

I've also raised three kids, built things on nights and weekends, started over more than once, and learned that I can't depend on having more time, more energy, or a perfectly functioning brain tomorrow.

So I don't.

I leave breadcrumbs for myself. I remove friction. I externalize what I can. I interrogate the problem before I admire the solution.

Tiny habits.

Repeated long enough that eventually they stopped looking tiny.

author: Britt Bowman
text:
Your workflow that looks so pretty in that deck is a lie. I learned this the hard way.

We had process maps, system configurations, dashboards, and automation. And our data was incorrectly mapped, aligned to outdated fields and values, or failed to pass altogether roughly 30% of the time.

So I stopped asking how the process was supposed to work and started asking people what they actually did when it broke.

"This says X, but when that happens I actually do Y."

"I know this account looks like that, but..."

"If Sales entered it this way, I fix it before..."

That's when I realized the documented process was never the real process. It was a linear, unidirectional version of how work moved under optimal conditions.

The real process had another layer underneath it.

People were interpreting, correcting, repeating steps, and making judgment calls. They knew which exception mattered and which didn't, and routed around problems nobody had bothered to document because everyone involved already knew what to do.

Except real processes are rarely linear, rarely unidirectional, and almost never happen under optimal conditions.

So we took what people knew and turned it into an actual operating model:

• Clear definitions, so everyone agreed on what the data meant
• Explicit ownership, so failures had a name attached
• Decision rules, so nobody reinvented the answer each time
• Feedback loops, so recurring errors became fixes, not folklore

Data misalignment went from roughly 30% to 0.61%.

That mattered when humans were running the workflow, but humans could compensate for what the system didn't know.

AI can't.

Your agent doesn't know about the spreadsheet someone keeps on their desktop. It doesn't know that step four actually happens three times because everyone on that one team needs to weigh in.

It doesn't know that when the system says X, Susan has known for eight years that it really means Y.

Unless you teach it.

That's the problem with automating the process you've documented rather than the one you actually run.

Humans have been carrying the missing context. AI exposes exactly how much of your operating model was living in their heads.

author: Britt Bowman
text:
I helped an organization recover ~$240MM in pipeline a few weeks ago. Not a single cent came from new leads. We found where the existing pipeline had been leaking.

The number was enormous, but the underlying problem wasn’t unique to an enterprise that size. I’ve seen the same pattern in midmarket companies, small businesses, and solopreneur operations.

The numbers change, but the leak doesn’t.

Companies are remarkably quick to decide they need more pipeline before figuring out what happened to the pipeline they already paid to create. So they buy more leads, launch another campaign, add another channel, or increase the spend.

But “we need more pipeline” can hide very different problems.

A targeting leak means the wrong people are entering the funnel.

A qualification leak means good opportunities are being filtered out, or bad ones are consuming resources.

A handoff leak means revenue is disappearing between teams, systems, or stages.

A conversion leak means the right opportunities are getting there, but they aren’t moving.

A retention leak means you’re replacing revenue you shouldn’t have lost in the first place.

Those aren’t five versions of the same problem. They all require different interventions.

If you don’t know which one you have, adding more volume can make the numbers look busier without fixing the constraint.

That’s the lesson I’ve learned after 20 years inside the systems connecting marketing, sales, operations, and revenue: Find the constraint before you fund the fix.

Don’t start with, “How do we generate more?” Start with, “Where does revenue stop moving, and what operating decision is causing it?”

I turned the framework into a practical Revenue Leak Map. I attached the summary here.

Save it for the next time someone says the answer is more pipeline.

If it surfaces a leak that’ll take more than a carousel to resolve, you know where to find me. More details in my profile and website.

author: Britt Bowman
text:
I've watched companies get very good at treating whatever revenue symptom (or whichever revenue leader) was screaming the loudest rather than fixing the root cause.

I've literally woken up in the middle of the night thinking about it. In fact, that's how I built the GTM SCALER framework, like an insane person, scribbling ideas on whatever scrap of paper I could find in the dark.

You know what I mean...

Pipeline fell, so run more campaigns. (Now now now!)

Conversion fell, so rewrite the messaging. (Don't give it time to land. New is always better!)

Sales cycles got longer, so add enablement. (The problem is Sales just doesn't get it, right?!?!)

AI underperforms, so obviously we need another tool. (AI POCitis much?)

The fix works for a second, and then six months later (if you're lucky), you're solving the same problem again.

We're diagnosing GTM problems based on where the symptom appeared, but the place where a problem shows up isn't necessarily where the system is breaking.

So I built GTM SCALER.

It diagnoses five dimensions of the GTM operating system at once: System, Credibility, Audience, Learnings, and Execution. These aren't steps. They're diagnostic dimensions because a pipeline problem might actually be an Audience problem. A conversion problem might originate in Credibility. An Execution problem can make a perfectly good strategy look wrong. And sometimes what looks like one tactical problem is several parts of the GTM system failing together.

Then comes the R: Route.

Route isn't scored. It's a separate decision layer that accounts for the company's context, urgency, authority, and readiness.

Because two companies can have nearly identical diagnostic scores and need completely different plans.

The score tells me what I'm looking at, but Route helps determine what to do about it.

After years of transformation work, I've learned that finding a problem isn't particularly difficult.

Finding the problem underneath the problem is where things get interesting.

author: Britt Bowman
text:
Knowledge17, May 2017. I'm Britt Champeau, a ServiceNow employee in a ServiceNow polo, being interviewed on the show floor about the platform and organizational change management.

Last week, August 2026. I'm Britt Bowman, sitting cross-legged on a folding lazy chair on the floor in my mother-in-law's Buddhist temple in Crestone, Colorado, about to jump on a client call for my own business (checking to see if my hair's gone flat with how dry it is).

In the nine years between those two photos, absolutely everything changed. I think most people will notice the physical difference first, and that's fine. I have definitely transformed in more ways than one, but that's not the story I want to tell.

The real gap between those two photos is about where my professional value lived.

In 2017, I was already ambitious and capable, but everything I could point to as proof of that lived inside ServiceNow. Over the years that followed, I got very good at making enormous, complicated systems work.

Whether I was leading global transformation programs, building GTM systems from scratch, or writing the code for an app with my own two hands, I was learning how to operate the machine. What I didn't understand yet was that the machine was never where the capability actually lived.

By 2026, I've figured that out. I'm not deploying my judgment inside one company's walls anymore. The judgment itself has become the work.

I now have my own frameworks, my own clients, and my own company. I advise companies navigating GTM and AI transformation, step into fractional leadership roles, build tools and assessments around the problems I keep seeing, and speak and write about what I'm learning along the way.

And the weirdest part is how little infrastructure any of that requires. There's no corporate office or anyone else's name on the door. Last week, all it took was a laptop, a folding lazy chair on the floor of a Buddhist temple in Crestone, and work that follows me wherever I happen to be sitting.

I don't think of this as an employee-to-entrepreneur transition. That framing is too small, and it makes the earlier version of me sound trapped.

She wasn't. That career built me. It gave me the reps, the scale, the proof that I could be trusted with something enormous.

It's closer to this. The institution gave me the platform, but in 2026 I carry it with me.

Britt Champeau was everything I needed her to be to become Britt Bowman. The transformation is that credibility has finally moved from the institution to me.

(And huge shoutout to my husband for having an easier-to-pronounce last name that makes me sound like a superhero... Peter Parker, Bruce Banner, Clark Kent, Sue Storm, Jessica Jones, Britt Bowman. Alliterative names for the win.)

author: Britt Bowman
text:
I'm sorry, but “start small” is terrible advice if you design the small thing to avoid everything that makes scale hard.

This advice is everywhere in AI and transformation circles: Pick a contained use case, run a pilot, prove ROI, get a quick win. Then scale.

Listen, I understand why it spread... It lowers the barrier to starting, gives nervous executives a safe bet, and probably produces a win.

But here's what companies actually do when they “start small”:

• They isolate the pilot from production data.
• They hand-pick the most motivated people.
• They manually work around broken processes.
• They create temporary governance that won't survive.
• They give the team executive air cover that won't exist at scale.

Then it succeeds, and everyone celebrates.

But it's not over.

When they try to scale it into the real organization, it hits shared data, conflicting definitions, existing workflows, security, ownership, and thousands of people who were never part of the experiment.

The “successful” pilot can't move. This is POCitis. Pilots that demo well but never reach production because the operating foundation was never part of the test.

My alternative: start narrow, not small.

Narrow the problem enough to learn quickly, but don't remove the conditions the solution will eventually have to survive. Use real data architecture, governance, users, and workflows.

That way, when it's successful, everyone has a real reason to celebrate.

author: Britt Bowman
text:
Thank you, Guillaume. That’s what I love about where Heracles’s story goes from here. At this point, the Argo is the mission. Jason is the leader. The Golden Fleece is the prize everyone is chasing. Being left behind should be a disaster.

Except Heracles goes on to have a story so much bigger than the Argo that most people don’t even remember he was an Argonaut.

There’s something wonderful about that. The voyage can be enormously important while you’re on it and still end up being a very small part of who you become.

author: Britt Bowman
text:
I think this is genuinely hard when you’re in the C-suite, Kyle. You got there in part because you have good ideas and good judgment, so it’s very easy to start believing yours are probably the best ideas in the room.

But if you’re an A player, you hire A players specifically because they know things you don’t. If you only want people who agree with you, you’re going to end up surrounded by C players pretty quickly.

Good for you for hiring A players and giving them the space to dissent

author: Britt Bowman
text:
For me it was campaign planning, Kelsey. I watched teams rebuild essentially the same planning process every quarter because every campaign looked different enough to convince us it was new work.

Once we separated what actually needed judgment from what was just the same scaffolding with different inputs, there was a ridiculous amount we could stop rebuilding.

author: Britt Bowman
text:
I used to worry that building a personal brand while I was employed would somehow look disloyal, Reggie, but most of the opportunities that came my way reflected well on the company too.

People wanted the person, but the company got to borrow the credibility. That seems like a pretty good trade while you have them.

author: Britt Bowman
text:
I think the uncomfortable part is that Marketing can’t fix a trust problem that the rest of the company keeps recreating, Irina.

You can tell the most accurate story in the world, but if the product, sales experience, employee experience, or customer experience contradicts it, people have way too many ways to find out now.

author: Britt Bowman
text: The funny part is I thought I was building the next chapter before I was forced to. I just thought I had another two years to do it. The ship had a different timeline.

author: Britt Bowman
text:
37 fractional clients sounds like my personal version of hell, Casey.

I want to know the business well enough to actually be useful, which means there’s a pretty hard ceiling on how many clients I can serve at once. Give me a handful of clients where I can go deep every time.

author: Britt Bowman
text:
I think a lot of companies are going to discover their AI dependencies for the first time when one of them changes underneath them, Guillaume.

A model changes, pricing moves, a provider changes its terms, access disappears, and suddenly something the business quietly built around one dependency doesn’t work anymore. I’d much rather have that conversation before we’re in the middle of it.

author: Britt Bowman
subject: Before you hire your first salesperson
text:
I worked with a founder who was trying to hire her first salesperson to break past $500,000. And when she did, growth got slower, not faster. She was so confused.

I watched this happen from the inside. At $500,000, everything had worked for her. Every lead came through LinkedIn, every proposal was customized, every customer conversation happened with the founder personally, and every follow-up lived in her head or in this ugly color-coded spreadsheet she swore she was going to clean up the following week but never had the time.

And it wasn’t because she was careless. It was because she’d built something from nothing and had to do everything at breakneck pace. There hadn’t been a reason up to that point to document how the company sold because the founder was always there. Of course she knew which prospects were serious, which objections mattered, where pricing could flex, and when a customer needed one more conversation before they were ready. She could feel the difference between a good opportunity and a distraction before anybody else could see it.

Then she hired someone to help carry the growth, and all of that hard-earned instinct became invisible because you can’t just mind-meld with someone and transfer years of judgment into their brain.

The salesperson didn’t know which prospects were qualified because the founder had never needed to define qualification. The messaging changed depending on who was on the call because the founder had always known how to adapt it. Pricing flexed based on a dozen signals she was processing without thinking about them. The salesperson kept asking perfectly reasonable questions, and the founder kept struggling to explain answers that had always felt obvious to her.

She’d hired someone to give her time back. Instead, she was spending more time reviewing emails, rewriting proposals, joining calls, and stepping into deals when they started to drift. The salesperson could feel that she wasn’t trusted, but she also knew she didn’t have enough information to make the decisions herself. The founder began to wonder whether she’d hired the wrong person. The salesperson began to wonder whether they’d accepted an impossible job.

Neither of them was failing. They were both working inside a system that only functioned when the founder was personally carrying it.

That’s the part of founder-led growth we don’t talk about enough. In the beginning, having one person hold the customer relationships, the pricing logic, the message, the follow-up, and the definition of a good opportunity is an enormous advantage. It lets the company learn quickly without stopping to explain itself. But the moment another person has to reproduce that success, the same advantage becomes a dependency.

The operating model that gets a founder to $500,000 can be built around instinct because the person with the instinct is always in the room. The operating model that gets the company to $1 million has to work when she isn’t.

And that doesn’t mean documenting every sentence she says or forcing her sales process into a fifty-page playbook no one will read. It means identifying the decisions the next person shouldn’t need her to make. What makes a lead worth pursuing? Which problems are a fit? When can pricing move? What information has to survive the handoff? When should someone keep working the opportunity, and when should they walk away?

That was the work this founder needed to do. She thought she was hiring capacity, but what the company needed first was a way to make her judgment transferable.

I wrote The Marketecture Mismatch because this problem changes shape as companies grow, but the underlying mistake stays the same. We keep adding people, platforms, and AI to a system that was never redesigned for the next stage, and then we blame the new thing when the old system can’t carry it.

Read The Marketecture Mismatch

Britt Bowman
Founder & Principal

author: Britt Bowman
subject: If your team keeps debating the number
text:
I once watched a leadership team spend forty-five minutes debating which dashboard was right. Sales had one number, marketing had another, finance had a third, and the executive sponsor kept opening tabs until she found the chart that supported the decision she already wanted to make.

Everyone does it. The tools all say something slightly different, so you pick the version of the truth that matches the call you already wanted to make, and you call it data-driven. It isn't. It's confirmation with a chart.

This is what “we need better reporting” almost always means. Not that the numbers are missing. That there are too many of them, none of them agree, and nobody owns which one is real. So the number stops being a decision tool and becomes a debating tool. Whoever argues best wins, not whoever's right.

The cost isn't the wrong dashboard. It's the slow decisions. Every choice now carries a tax. Reconcile the numbers. Litigate the definitions. Build consensus on what's even true before you can move. A company that trusts its numbers decides and acts. A company that doesn't decides, then spends a week defending the decision to itself.

Here's the reframe. You don't have a data problem. You have a trust problem, and trust doesn't come from a better dashboard. It comes from shared definitions everyone signs, evidence people can see, clear ownership of each number, and the judgment to know which one matters for the call in front of you. Miss any of those and the number stays a matter of opinion.

So here's the question. If your team wrote down your most important number and its definition, separately, would the answers match? If you're not sure, that's the finding. That gap is where your decisions are leaking speed.

author: Britt Bowman
subject: If the playbook used to work and now it doesn't
text:
There's a point where the growth playbook that built the company starts making everyone look less capable than they are. The founder thinks the team isn't executing with enough urgency. The team thinks the strategy keeps changing. Marketing is driving activity, sales is working the leads, and everyone is tired of being told to go back to the thing that worked two years ago.

The maddening part is that the old playbook wasn't bad. It had opened a market, filled the pipeline, and helped the company become the thing it is now. But it was built for a smaller business with fewer products, shorter handoffs, and leaders who could settle a disagreement by walking across the room.

By the time the company tried to reuse it, there were more channels, more people, more exceptions, and three different definitions of a qualified opportunity. The same tactic produced more meetings and less movement, not because everyone had forgotten how to execute, but because the operating model around the tactic had changed without being redesigned.

That's what makes a once-successful playbook so hard to retire. It carries proof. Someone can point to the quarter it worked and treat that history as evidence that it should work now. But a tactic doesn't scale on its own. It depends on the company around it, and the company is no longer the one that made the playbook successful.

Before you fund another run, ask what conditions made it work the first time. Who owned the decision? Which handoffs were simple? What did the buyer expect? Which exceptions did the team handle manually because everyone involved still fit in one room?

If those conditions have changed, repeating the tactic isn't discipline. It's nostalgia with a budget.

author: Britt Bowman
subject: If every decision still runs through you
text:
I worked with a founder whose calendar looked like a crime scene. Every customer exception, pricing question, hiring decision, product tradeoff, and marketing approval landed on her desk because she was the person who knew why the company had made every decision in the first place.

She kept saying she needed a better calendar system. What she needed was a company that could make more decisions without borrowing her memory.

The meetings weren't random. Each one marked a place where ownership, context, or decision rights had never fully left the founder. The team was capable, but capability doesn't help when no one knows which call they are allowed to make, what information governs it, or how far their authority extends.

That's why founder bottlenecks rarely feel like control problems from the inside. They feel like responsibility. The founder answers because the customer needs an answer, reviews because quality matters, and steps in because waiting would be worse. Every intervention is reasonable. Together, they teach the company that the safest operating model is to keep routing through one person.

Look at your calendar for the last two weeks and circle every meeting that existed because someone needed your judgment to move. Then sort those decisions into three groups: only I can make this, someone else can make this with a clear rule, and someone else should already own this.

The third group is where your calendar is telling you the org chart is wrong.

author: Britt Bowman
subject: Your GTM transformation shouldn't start with a tool
text:
I love good technology. I really do.

Give me a powerful platform, a clever AI capability, or a workflow that suddenly makes something possible and I will get genuinely excited about it.

But your GTM transformation shouldn’t start with the tool.

It should start with the thing your revenue engine needs to become capable of doing that it cannot do reliably today.

Maybe customer context disappears between marketing and sales. Maybe leaders can’t trust the forecast because every team defines the stages differently. Maybe the organization can generate buying signals but has no consistent way to turn them into action. Maybe an AI pilot works beautifully while five teams disagree about who would own it in production.

Those are not software-selection problems. They’re operating-model problems.

The tool matters, of course. But it sits inside a larger system of ownership, decisions, definitions, data, workflows, incentives, and measurement. If that system stays the same, the new technology usually makes the existing confusion move faster.

This is why so many transformation programs feel incredibly busy without becoming meaningfully different. The implementation launches. The training happens. The dashboard goes live. Everyone celebrates the milestone.

And the work still moves through the organization exactly the way it did before.

A better starting point is to define the operating capability first.

What outcome needs to become repeatable? Who owns it? Which decisions have to move? What information has to travel with the work? What standard defines success? Where can AI improve the capability, and where does the organization itself need to change?

Once that’s clear, choosing and deploying the technology gets so much more interesting. You’re no longer asking what the tool can do. You’re designing what the business will finally be able to do because the whole operating model can support it.

That’s the transformation.
